title: Making records with Jelly Roll Morton and what kind of man he was
summary: Wilson recorded about ten sides with Morton between jobs and found him nice to work for; he recalls personnel and his favorite, The Pearls.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: I see. Well, can we back up a little bit? Who were you playing with when you made the records with Jelly Roll?
That was in between engagements, but Art Simms, in Milwaukee. Because I wasn't working.
You were about 18 at that time?
Yeah.
19, something like that.
Something like that.
Did you work with Jelly on anything other than the recordings?
No.

Tell me about him. There's been a lot of stories about him, how he would put the band together, and being somewhat of an odd character. In later years he bragged about, you know, coming up from New Orleans, and so on, showing the Chicago guys a thing or two, because he bragged a lot. But what kind of guy was he?
Well, I found him to be very nice. I never had any problems with him.
How did he call you --
He called me -- I don't know how he happened to call me for that record session. I don't know who recommended me to him.
Dodds Brothers were on that?
Yeah.
And George Mitchell?
George Mitchell.
And one of the --
Kid Ory on trombone.
I think one of the Reeves Brothers (PHONETIC) was on --
Some of them, yeah.
Ruben Reeves?
Ruben Reeves, yeah.
On trombone?
Yeah. We had different personnel on -- I made about ten sides with Jelly.
Yeah, I was looking at two sections last night, the one where he made "Wild Man" and "Jungle Blues", and --
Yeah.
And one of my favorite Jelly compositions, "The Pearls."
Yeah, that's my -- that was my favorite. You'd be surprised, that's probably the only one I really remember out of the whole session, "The Pearls." Oh, man. Yeah.
Yeah, well, that was a piano piece, originally. How did he -- did he write out the music, or did he just sing the part?
Yeah, he wrote it. He wrote the music, yeah.
He wrote out the music for all the horns?
For all the horns.
Well, how did he rehearse the band? Did you rehearse in the studios, or someplace else?
In the studio. For -- you know, during the session.
Yeah. Well, how did he -- how did
he work?

Well, he just -- when you started rehearsing, we just rehearsed the first tune we were going to record. We'd run it down, and rehearse it and get it down, timing and everything. And after we got it down, we'd just go ahead and record it.
